claims.text: Existing high-entropy-alloy intermediate layers are optimized for mechanical robustness.
Existing high-entropy-alloy intermediate layers have suboptimal thermal conductivity.
Nanometer-scale surface modification can produce an ultra-thin coherent interfacial layer on a high-entropy-alloy intermediate layer.
The engineered interfacial layer will improve the connectivity of thermal-transport paths.
The ultra-thin coherent interfacial layer will be located at grain boundaries.
The coherent interfacial layer will reduce phonon scattering at grain boundaries.
The coherent interfacial layer will reduce electron scattering at grain boundaries.
Reduced phonon and electron scattering will create continuous, low-resistance thermal-conduction paths.
The surface modification will not alter the bulk alloy composition.
Preserving the bulk composition will preserve the alloy's mechanical strength.
The modified alloy will have higher thermal conductivity than the unmodified intermediate layer.
The modified alloy will maintain high strength and ductility.
The proposed benefit should persist at 600–1000°C under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
Temperatures of 600–1000°C and the specified cyclic loads are typical of plasma-facing reactor environments.
Current high-entropy-alloy intermediate layers prioritize mechanical integrity but have limited heat-transfer performance.
The magnitude of any thermal-conductivity improvement is uncertain.
Long-term stability of the engineered layer under reactor irradiation and particle-flux conditions remains unvalidated.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis promises improved heat-transfer capability, whereas the predicted outcome allows performance merely comparable to current intermediate layers; comparability would not establish improvement.

The intervention is described as surface modification, but the mediator is placed at internal grain boundaries; no processing route is given that connects a surface treatment to grain-boundary-wide interfacial-layer formation.
